transcript: Carrie Coon is giving one of the best performances of the season in bug, a play that is finally debuting on Broadway 30 years after its initial premiere. And I have to say, for a play that was written 30 years ago, it does feel surprisingly contemporary. It follows Carrie Coon's character Agnes, and her budding relationship with Peter, played by Namir Smallwood, who we later find out is schizophrenic and off his meds. as he begins slipping further and further into his own hallucinations, so too does Carrie Coon's character, despite the fact that she does not have schizophrenia. And I think that's what makes this play so interesting and also feel so topical. It shows how a quote, unquote normal person can fall into these rabbit holes and slowly begin to buy into these otherwise unbelievable conspiracy theories. Peter's hallucinations begin with just a bug, then it's two bugs, then it's an entire infestation. And that slowly snowballs into an entire government conspiracy. And it's that gradual descent that makes it so dangerous. And every time we see her start to doubt this narrative, she inevitably pulls herself even deeper into it. Cause it is easier to accept this fake reality then the actual reality that she was misled by this man or that this man that she potentially loves is mentally ill. And as you might imagine, this does make for a rather uncomfortable play. These characters are not likable, and we are watching them make Decisions that, at least on the surface, seem incredibly logical. But the play is not asking us to forgive these characters or to like these characters. It is simply asking you to see them and to understand why they are making these decisions, even if you may not like the decisions that they're making. And in a time of rampant misinformation, where it is very easy to look across the aisle and say, I have no idea how these people could possibly believe this thing, I think that a play exploring how a person can be essentially brainwashed actually feels pretty vital.
